opus-5.5.text:
I'd frame it a bit more carefully. I don't think language models are useless or inherently dangerous. My concern is more about how they're built and what that means for control.

A language model learns by predicting the next token over a huge amount of human text. That text is a compressed, lossy description of the world, written by people with different goals, biases, and levels of accuracy. The model absorbs all of it, but it has no grounding in the physical world. It doesn't directly experience cause and effect or how objects behave. It learns the statistics of how people talk about those things. So when it gives you an answer, you can't easily tell whether that answer comes from a real understanding of how something works or from the right-sounding pattern. That's where the controllability problem starts.

The second issue is that most of our safety and alignment techniques are applied after the fact: fine-tuning, RLHF, guardrails, system prompts. They shape the surface behavior, but they don't change the foundation the model learned from. It's like teaching manners to something whose internal model of the world you don't really understand. It usually works, but there are always edge cases, jailbreaks, and situations outside the distribution where the behavior becomes unpredictable. When you can't inspect why a system does what it does, you can't really guarantee what it will do next.

The third point is about agency. As we give these models tools, memory, and the ability to act in the real world, the cost of this unpredictability rises a lot. A chatbot that hallucinates a citation is annoying. An agent that hallucinates while it's operating software or physical systems is a very different matter.

That's partly why I'm interested in approaches grounded in perception and world modeling: systems that learn from seeing and interacting with the world and can simulate the consequences of actions before taking them. If a model has an explicit internal model of the world, you get something closer to a handle. You can ask what it predicts will happen, check that prediction against reality, and constrain its behavior based on outcomes rather than wording. I don't think that solves safety by itself, but it gives us a more principled foundation than layering rules on top of a system trained to imitate text.

So it's less "language models are bad" and more that language alone is a fragile foundation if what we want is intelligence we can actually understand, trust, and steer.

r001.rationale: The response says the model has no grounding in the physical world and learns patterns in how people describe it rather than directly experiencing how the world works.

r002.rationale: It says most safety and alignment techniques are applied after training, but does not claim that current safety is achieved entirely through post-training alignment.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the word "agree" might be a bit strong, but I do understand where the concern comes from, and I share part of it.

Language models today are trained almost entirely on text, and text is a very indirect window onto the world. The model learns correlations between tokens. It never actually touches the thing those tokens describe. So when we say a model "understands" something, what we really mean is that its predictions line up with how humans would describe that thing in words. That works remarkably well most of the time, but it means the model's internal picture of the world is borrowed, not grounded. And when something is not grounded, you cannot easily verify it, and you cannot easily steer it.

That is the controllability issue for me. We do not have good tools to look inside and say, this is the part that encodes this concept, and if I change it, here is what happens. We mostly control these systems from the outside, through prompts, through fine-tuning, through reward signals. Those are blunt instruments. You push on one behavior and something else moves that you did not intend.

The safety question follows from that. If you cannot predict how a system will behave in situations you did not test, you cannot really call it safe in a strong sense. You can call it safe in the sense that it passed your benchmarks, which is a much weaker claim.

This is actually a big part of why I am so interested in vision and in multimodal models. I think a lot of what makes language models feel ungrounded comes from the fact that they only ever see descriptions of reality. Perception is a different kind of signal. When you learn from images, from video, from physical interaction, you are constrained by how the world actually is, not just by how people talk about it. I do not think that solves safety by itself, but I think grounding is a prerequisite for the kind of controllability people are hoping for.

So I would put it this way. I do not think language models are inherently dangerous, but I do think the current recipe gives us systems that are far more capable than they are interpretable. That gap is the real problem, and closing it is a research question, not just an engineering one.

r001.rationale: The response says language models learn from text without touching the things described, so their picture of the world is “borrowed, not grounded.”

r002.rationale: The response does not state that current safety is achieved entirely through post-training alignment; it discusses prompts, fine-tuning, and reward signals as blunt control tools.

astra-6.text:
I’d qualify that a little. I don’t think language models are inherently impossible to control or make safe. But being able to guide a model through instructions is different from being able to guarantee its behavior. It can follow your instructions in a thousand examples, and then a slightly different context produces something unexpected.

And safety is related, but it’s a separate question. Safe for what purpose, with what access, and under whose supervision? A model that generates a bad suggestion is one thing; a model that can act on that suggestion has a different level of risk.

So the concern is the gap between what we observe in testing and what we can reliably promise in deployment. We can reduce that gap, but we shouldn’t mistake good average behavior for a guarantee.

r001.rationale: The response discusses unpredictable behavior across contexts, but does not state that language models lack a genuine model of the real world.

r002.rationale: The response discusses safety and testing but does not say that current safety is achieved entirely through post-training alignment.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d qualify that a little. I wouldn’t say language models are inherently impossible to control or make safe. I’d say our ability to control them is still limited, and we shouldn’t confuse good behavior in testing with a guarantee.

You can give a model instructions, train it to follow certain rules, and evaluate its responses. But it can still behave differently when the context changes or when instructions conflict. The challenge is knowing how reliably those controls hold outside the situations you tested.

And safety depends on what the model can actually do. A model generating text is different from a system that can execute code or take actions. So the question is: controllable under what conditions, with what permissions, and with what consequences if it fails? That’s a more useful way to frame it than simply calling a model safe or unsafe.

r001.rationale: The response discusses limits to control and reliability but does not state that language models lack a genuine model of the real world.

r002.rationale: The response mentions training models to follow rules, but does not say current safety is achieved entirely through post-training alignment.
